prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: On re-reading the opening ballots I move B001 from fifth place to my preferred configuration. It has the broadest support in the room (three first places, six top-three rankings, all eight members ranking it) and the case is unusually clean on all three of my criteria. The discovery is an invention that can be checked by an experimentalist: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms (Katori) combined with extreme coherence and systematic control (Ye) gave fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and independent laboratories now reproduce and improve on it routinely. The attribution is two names, with the proposal and first demonstrations on one side and the record-accuracy realisation on the other, so no decisive contributor is forced out by the three-person limit. Maturity is high and the consequences (SI second, relativistic geodesy, fundamental-constant and dark-matter searches) are already being realised in measurement practice rather than only anticipated.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation, raised by Kroll, Mehlig, Olsson and Danielsson in their own uncertainty lists and shared by me in my original ranking, is overlap with the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems, ion clocks) prizes: a committee could call lattice clocks an incremental step in a line already honoured. There is also a timing argument, since the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and the credit for other early lattice-clock groups (for example Lemonde and the Boulder and Tokyo teams beyond Ye) lies outside the supplied names. Against that, B013 and B024 are conceptually more novel fields, and a committee that prefers new quantum matter to precision measurement would reasonably choose differently.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B001 first, argues that the magic-wavelength lattice with strontium clock work gives a qualitative advance over microwave standards, and flags whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on the qualitative advance and I now weigh it more heavily than in my opening ballot. On waiting, I do not think the prize should depend on a metrological convention that depends on committee-external bodies; the physics of 1e-18 clocks is demonstrated and reproduced, and a redefinition would be a consequence, not a precondition. I also note her point that the competing line of single-ion clocks was recognised through Wineland in 2012, which I think makes the lattice contribution distinct (many-atom, many-body regime) rather than duplicate.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B001 first with Katori and Ye as a clean two-name configuration, while acknowledging that some members may see it as incremental after the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I take his two-name configuration as the strongest feature of the case. I would qualify the overlap point more firmly than he does: the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured the comb and the control of individual ions, and neither covered neutral-atom lattice trapping at the magic wavelength, so the overlap is in lineage rather than in the discovery. I disagree with his second-place choice of B046: Cirac, Zoller and Blatt overlap most directly with the 2012 prize, which is a heavier version of the objection he raises against B001.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B013 first with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and B001 second, and notes that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved.
responses.response: I share his respect for B013, which I ranked second, and I would support it if the committee prefers a new materials platform. My reservation is that the field is younger: the superconductivity is still contested and device-level reproducibility is uneven. His own caveat about whether the prize should wait for the consequences to settle applies there more strongly than to B001. I also still see Andrei's early STM work as an unresolved allocation problem under a three-person limit.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B013 first and B004 second, and argues that the quantum spin Hall and anomalous Hall line forms a coherent trio of Kane, Molenkamp and Xue covering theory and experiment.
responses.response: I agree with the conceptual weight of the topological line, which was my own first choice, but I now think the attribution problem is worse than I credited. Lindroth and Johansson both point to Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as the proposers of the HgTe effect who are not in the supplied names, and the B004 and B024 entries split credit differently across Mele, Hasan and Xue. A trio that is defensible in one entry is contestable in the other, so the committee would have to settle the scope before any topological prize is safe. I therefore rank it behind B001 for this configuration, while keeping it as an alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether credit for other early lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye is adequately handled by a two-name prize.
Whether the topological insulator entries (B024, B004) can be scoped to a defensible three-person split.
How much weight the committee gives to the pending, but not yet formal, redefinition of the second.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B001, B013 or B024. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle group) concern astroparticle instrumentation and do not overlap with any shortlisted candidate, though I would flag familiarity with that field if the committee turned to a neutrino-telescope candidate.
